cues.text: A Senator's Education
Born around 354 at Bordeaux into a distinguished Aquitanian family, Paulinus received an outstanding classical education under the celebrated poet Ausonius, one of the finest teachers of the age.

He rose rapidly through the Roman civil service, becoming suffect consul and then governor of Campania, in southern Italy, while still a young man — a career trajectory that marked him for the very highest offices of the empire.
Conversion and Marriage
Despite his worldly success, Paulinus grew increasingly restless in public life, and around 389 he married a devout Spanish Christian noblewoman named Therasia .

Baptized alongside his brother by Bishop Delphinus of Bordeaux, and further influenced by St. Martin of Tours , who cured him of an eye ailment, Paulinus's Christian faith deepened steadily through the 380s.
Renouncing a Fortune
The death of their only child, born and dying within eight days in 392, proved a turning point.
Paulinus and Therasia resolved to withdraw entirely from worldly life.
They sold their substantial estates in Gaul and Spain, distributing the proceeds to the poor.
This renunciation was so complete and startling to Roman aristocratic sensibilities that his old teacher Ausonius wrote him verses of bewildered reproach.
Paulinus replied with dignified poetic epistles of his own.
A New Life at Nola
Ordained a priest at Barcelona in 394 despite his own hesitation, Paulinus and Therasia settled the following year near the shrine of the martyr St. Felix at Nola, in Campania.
There, Paulinus devoted himself to asceticism, hospitality to pilgrims, and ransoming captives and prisoners with what remained of his resources.
Around 409 he was chosen bishop of Nola by popular acclaim, an office he held for over twenty years.
A Christian Poet
Paulinus became one of the foremost Christian Latin poets of his era, composing an annual cycle of poems in honor of St. Felix each year from 395 to 407.
He also wrote numerous letters to the leading Christian figures of his day — Augustine , Jerome , Sulpicius Severus, and others.
As the Catholic Encyclopedia notes, his letters were so thoroughly saturated with Scripture that he seemed to live and write entirely in its spirit.
Legacy
Paulinus died at Nola on 22 June 431, remembered as one of the great examples of Christian renunciation among the late Roman aristocracy.
He set aside senatorial rank, wealth, and a promising public career for poverty, prayer, and devoted pastoral care.
He left behind poetry treasured by later generations and a model of episcopal charity long celebrated by the Church.
